paragraphs: Second-order recurrent neural networks model sequences using richer interactions than ordinary recurrent networks. These interactions give them greater expressive power, but their parameters form a large tensor that makes computation difficult. The paper studies whether a compact tensor representation can retain useful modeling capacity while making better use of a limited parameter budget.

The resulting model, CPRNN, represents this tensor through CP decomposition. Two design choices become central: the decomposition rank and the size of the hidden state. The authors analyze how these choices affect capacity and establish relationships among ordinary RNNs, second-order RNNs, interaction-restricted MIRNNs, and CPRNNs. This connects compression choices to what the models can represent.

Experiments on Penn Treebank support the analysis: with a fixed parameter budget and an appropriate combination of rank and hidden size, CPRNNs outperform the other three model families. The qualification matters because compression alone is not the reported explanation for success. The contribution is a theoretical and empirical account of how to allocate parameters within a richer recurrent architecture.
icml-2024-a-tensor-decomposition-perspec.tldr: CPRNN uses tensor decomposition to make second-order recurrent networks compact, with strong results when rank and hidden size are chosen appropriately.

paragraphs: A public model supplies predictions that many downstream agents use to make decisions. Those agents can have different objectives, so improving prediction accuracy alone may not serve them equally well. This paper treats predictions as a service and asks how training should account for the different outcomes that users of that service actually care about.

The authors introduce an Equitable Objective and pair it with a policy gradient training algorithm. The objective incorporates downstream agents’ concerns and aims to make their performance distribution more uniform. This changes the training target: the model is assessed through the consequences of its predictions for heterogeneous agents, bringing disparities between those agents into the optimization process.

The paper provides theoretical analysis and empirical case studies supporting improved performance equity among agents using the shared model. The stated result concerns how performance is distributed across those agents. It gives a concrete approach to incorporating downstream objectives into public-model training, instead of relying on predictive accuracy alone to capture whether the service benefits its different users equitably.
icml-2024-building-socially-equitable-pu.tldr: An Equitable Objective trains shared public models to distribute performance more evenly across downstream agents with different goals.

paragraphs: Backdoor attacks cause a language model to change its decisions when particular triggers appear. Triggers can involve words, sentences, grammar, or style, making defenses tied to a specific trigger form difficult to generalize. FABE approaches this problem through causal inference, aiming to separate legitimate relationships between meaning and predictions from associations introduced by an attacker.

The framework uses an additional fine-tuned language model to produce text with the same meaning as the original input. This text serves as the causal ‘front door’ through which the defense reasons about the input and the model’s decision. The method avoids assumptions about trigger form, while its causal construction still depends on following the front-door criterion and adjustment formula.

In experiments covering token, sentence, and syntactic attacks, FABE reduces attack success from 93.63% to 15.12%. Ablation studies examine the contribution of its modules and support the importance of the causal requirements. These findings indicate substantial protection across the tested attack forms, with the semantic intermediary and causal adjustment jointly central to the reported defense.
icml-2024-causality-based-front-door-def.tldr: FABE uses a meaning-preserving text intermediary and causal adjustment to reduce language-model backdoor attacks without assuming a particular trigger form.

paragraphs: Visual applications such as 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis need representations that combine quality with compact storage. Tensor networks offer a promising way to obtain both, but learning their parameters can be difficult. The paper focuses on tensor trains, whose particularly compact representation has been held back by challenges in optimization.

The proposed method, Prolongation Upsampling Tensor Train, or PuTT, learns through a sequence of increasingly fine representations. It starts with a coarse tensor train, upsamples the learned representation, and continues refining it. This makes the progression from coarse structure to finer detail part of the learning procedure, addressing the optimization problem alongside the choice of representation.

The authors evaluate compression, denoising, and image completion using image fitting, 3D fitting, and novel view synthesis tasks. PuTT shows improved performance over state-of-the-art tensor-based methods in these evaluations. The findings support coarse-to-fine learning as a useful way to realize more of tensor trains’ potential: their value depends on being able to fit them effectively as well as store them compactly.
icml-2024-coarse-to-fine-tensor-trains-f.tldr: PuTT learns compact tensor-train visual representations by repeatedly upsampling and refining them from coarse to fine.

paragraphs: Multi-label learning allows an example to have several labels, whose relationships can help prediction. When only a small amount of labeled data is available, however, those relationships are difficult to estimate reliably. This paper addresses how to use label dependence in semi-supervised learning, where unlabeled examples also contribute to training.

The proposed PCLP method infers a correlation-induced label prior to improve pseudo-labels, the provisional labels assigned during learning. It constructs a prior probability distribution using a structural causal model, then constrains the correlations among generated pseudo-labels to agree with that prior. The approach incorporates these constraints into a variational label-enhancement framework trained jointly on labeled and unlabeled examples.

The authors provide theoretical results concerning pseudo-label accuracy and learning consistency, and report superior performance across several benchmark datasets. The key contribution is the route through which label relationships enter training: a structured prior guides pseudo-label generation when direct correlation estimation from scarce labeled data is unreliable. The reported results support that approach as a way to make unlabeled examples more useful.
icml-2024-correlation-induced-label-prio.tldr: PCLP uses a causal-model-based label prior to guide pseudo-label relationships when labeled multi-label data is scarce.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student model using a teacher model’s responses. For object detection, one common approach asks the student to imitate the teacher’s feature maps. This paper examines a complication: the gap between those maps varies across regions, reflecting different levels of student ability and different learning difficulties.

Disparity Feature Distillation, or DFD, applies different constraints to regions with different degrees of teacher–student disagreement. Its central idea is to combine stricter and more lenient treatment within the same distillation process. The authors argue that accounting for uneven disparities helps the student absorb the teacher’s knowledge more effectively than treating the entire feature map uniformly.

For ResNet50-based RetinaNet, FasterRCNN, and RepPoints detectors, reported mAP rises from 37.4%, 38.4%, and 38.6% to 41.7%, 42.4%, and 42.7%, respectively. The paper also reports substantial improvements for YOLO and vision-transformer-based models. These experiments support the practical value of adapting distillation constraints to local learning difficulty across several detector architectures, rather than viewing every teacher–student difference as an equivalent training signal.
icml-2024-dfd-distilling-the-feature-dis.tldr: DFD improves detector distillation by applying different constraints to feature regions with different teacher–student disparities.

paragraphs: Evaluating a reinforcement learning policy often means running it repeatedly and averaging the outcomes. These online Monte Carlo estimates are useful for comparing design choices, but acquiring enough environment interactions can be costly. This paper seeks more data-efficient evaluation while preserving unbiasedness, so the estimator still targets the policy’s actual expected performance.

The authors derive a tailored behavior policy, which controls how evaluation data is collected, in closed form. They prove that this policy reduces estimator variance, then develop algorithms to learn it from previously collected offline data. The offline information therefore helps shape new interactions, connecting existing experience to the efficiency of subsequent online evaluation.

The theory also characterizes how errors in learning the behavior policy affect the amount of variance reduction. That connection matters because practical use relies on a learned version of the ideal policy. Experiments show better performance than previous methods across a broader set of environments, with fewer offline-data requirements. Together, these results support designing data collection specifically for accurate, efficient policy evaluation.
icml-2024-efficient-policy-evaluation-wi.tldr: Offline data helps learn a behavior policy that reduces the variance of unbiased online policy evaluation.

paragraphs: Heuristics provide practical ways to tackle difficult search and optimization problems, but designing them manually can require substantial expertise and labor. Evolution of Heuristics, or EoH, combines language models with evolutionary computation to automate that design process. Its central move is to represent an algorithm’s idea as well as its executable implementation.

EoH expresses heuristic ideas in natural language, calling them thoughts, and uses a language model to translate those thoughts into code. An evolutionary search then develops both the thoughts and the code. This gives the search two connected representations to work with: a description of the strategy and a program that carries it out.

Experiments on three combinatorial optimization benchmarks show EoH outperforming commonly used handcrafted heuristics and recent automatic-design approaches, including FunSearch. For online bin packing, the authors report that a heuristic produced with relatively few language-model queries significantly exceeds widely used human-designed baselines. These findings support the usefulness of evolving verbal ideas alongside implementations, with query efficiency forming an explicit part of the reported advantage.
icml-2024-evolution-of-heuristics-toward.tldr: EoH evolves natural-language heuristic ideas and executable code together to automate effective algorithm design.

paragraphs: Federated learning involves clients whose hardware may differ substantially in available computing resources. Assigning different smaller models can help weaker devices participate, but combining those heterogeneous models can degrade the global result. FedLMT addresses this tension by reducing resource requirements while giving clients a common model structure to train.

The framework assigns a homogeneous model that has already been factorized into a low-rank form. This reduces computation and communication without requiring aggregation across heterogeneous sub-models. The authors theoretically establish that convergence of the low-rank model can guarantee convergence of the original full model. This supplies a formal connection between training the compact representation and the underlying model.

For clients with more individualized resource needs, the paper extends the approach to pFedLMT, separating parameters into shared and custom components. Experiments support the theoretical analysis and show both methods outperforming comparison baselines with substantially lower computation and communication costs. The contribution combines a resource-saving model representation, compatible aggregation, and convergence analysis to address the participation and performance challenges caused by hardware diversity.
icml-2024-fedlmt-tackling-system-heterog.tldr: FedLMT uses shared low-rank models to reduce federated-training costs while avoiding heterogeneous aggregation and providing convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: In-context learning teaches a language model a task through examples included in its prompt. Those demonstrations occupy context space, and their influence can be difficult to adjust quantitatively. This paper proposes encoding the demonstrations into an in-context vector, or ICV, that can guide the model through its internal representations.

The method first runs demonstration examples through the model and constructs a vector from its latent embeddings. For a new query, that vector shifts the model’s latent states, so the demonstrations need not appear in the prompt. Adjusting the vector’s magnitude provides a direct control over the strength of this intervention, while vector arithmetic can combine different instruction types.

The authors report better performance than standard in-context learning and fine-tuning on tasks involving safety, style transfer, role-playing, and formatting. They also describe the approach as substantially more computationally efficient than fine-tuning. The findings support using demonstration-derived internal signals as a practical means of steering behavior, with shorter prompts, adjustable influence, and the demonstrated ability to combine instructions.
icml-2024-in-context-vectors-making-in-c.tldr: In-context vectors compress demonstrations into internal steering signals whose strength and combinations can be adjusted.

paragraphs: Language models store attention keys and values in a cache to avoid recomputing them during generation. This cache grows with context length and batch size, increasing memory use and data movement. KIVI addresses this serving bottleneck by reducing the numerical precision of cached values, allowing the cache to occupy fewer bytes.

The paper first examines the distributions of cache elements in popular models. Its finding is asymmetric: keys should be quantized per channel, while values should be quantized per token. KIVI turns that distinction into a tuning-free, two-bit quantization algorithm with a hardware-friendly implementation. Treating the two cache components differently is the design choice motivated by the distribution study.

For Llama and Llama-2, Falcon, and Mistral models, the authors report nearly unchanged quality with 2.6 times lower peak memory usage, counting model weights as well. The reduced memory requirement permits up to four times larger batches and delivers 2.35–3.47 times throughput on real inference workloads. These results connect cache-aware quantization directly to practical serving capacity.
icml-2024-kivi-a-tuning-free-asymmetric-.tldr: KIVI quantizes attention keys and values differently at two bits, reducing memory and increasing serving throughput while largely preserving quality.

paragraphs: Many learning problems involve moving a collection of particles so that its distribution better matches a target distribution. Wasserstein gradient flow provides a way to move those particles while reducing an f-divergence, a measure of statistical discrepancy. Implementing that movement requires a velocity field specifying how the particles should change.

Earlier approaches estimate a density ratio between the particle and target distributions, then differentiate the estimate to obtain velocities. The paper identifies a possible weakness in this sequence: overfitting the ratio can make the resulting velocity estimates inaccurate. Drawing inspiration from nonparametric curve fitting, the authors instead estimate the velocity fields directly through interpolation.

The authors prove consistency of their estimators under mild conditions and demonstrate their effectiveness in domain adaptation and missing-data imputation. The theoretical claim is conditional on those conditions, while the applications establish empirical usefulness in the tested settings. The contribution targets the quantity needed to move particles directly, addressing a source of error in the intermediate ratio-estimation approach.
icml-2024-minimizing-f-divergences-by-in.tldr: Directly interpolating particle velocity fields offers a consistent, condition-dependent alternative to differentiating estimated density ratios.

paragraphs: MobileLLM investigates language models with fewer than a billion parameters for on-device applications motivated by cloud costs and latency. The paper emphasizes architecture as a significant determinant of quality at this scale. Its question is how to use a small parameter budget effectively enough to support practical language-model tasks.

The baseline combines deep, thin networks with shared embeddings and grouped-query attention. A further variant, MobileLLM-LS, introduces immediate block-wise weight sharing without increasing model size and with only marginal latency overhead. These choices organize and reuse the available parameters, making network design a central part of the approach to compact models.

The authors report accuracy gains of 2.7% and 4.3% over preceding 125M- and 350M-parameter state-of-the-art models, with weight sharing adding 0.7% and 0.8%. The family also improves on prior sub-billion models in chat benchmarks and approaches LLaMA-v2 7B correctness on API-calling tasks. That latter finding concerns a specific application, supporting the potential of small models for common on-device use cases.
icml-2024-mobilellm-optimizing-sub-billi.tldr: MobileLLM shows that carefully designed architectures and weight sharing can improve sub-billion-parameter models for on-device tasks.

paragraphs: Neural operators learn mappings between functions, making them useful for scientific problems such as predicting solutions of partial differential equations. Fourier neural operators use global operations that can oversmooth local details. This paper develops local operator layers that preserve the ability to make predictions at different resolutions while capturing finer spatial information.

The authors pursue two constructions. One learns differential operators, proving that appropriately scaling CNN kernel values yields such operators, inspired by stencil methods. The other learns integral operators with locally supported kernels using suitable basis representations. Both constructions retain the properties of operator learning, bringing local processing into a framework that supports prediction at any resolution.

Adding these layers to Fourier neural operators reduces relative L2 error by 34–72% in the reported experiments, which include turbulent two-dimensional Navier–Stokes and spherical shallow-water equations. The results support combining global and local operations for these scientific modeling tasks. The theoretical constructions explain how local layers can fit the operator setting, while the experiments show their practical contribution to accuracy.
icml-2024-neural-operators-with-localize.tldr: Local differential and integral operator layers improve Fourier neural operators while preserving prediction across resolutions.

paragraphs: Shuffling gradient methods include Random Reshuffle, Shuffle Once, and Incremental Gradient. Although widely used, their practical performance has been only partly explained by convergence theory. This paper focuses on the final iterate produced by optimization and asks how quickly its objective value approaches the optimum, a criterion distinct from distance to an optimal solution.

Previous results covered averaged iterates for convex objectives and final iterates for strongly convex problems using squared distance. Those guarantees did not adequately explain final-iterate performance measured through the objective-value gap in settings such as constrained optimization. The authors establish last-iterate convergence rates for this gap even without requiring strong convexity.

The new bounds either nearly match existing last-iterate lower bounds or match the speed of previous best upper bounds for averaged iterates. This gives a stronger theoretical account of the final result returned by shuffling methods. The contribution is specifically about convergence guarantees and their performance criterion: it connects the final iterate’s objective value to rates previously unavailable under the studied conditions.
icml-2024-on-the-last-iterate-convergenc.tldr: The paper establishes objective-value convergence rates for the final iterate of shuffling gradient methods without requiring strong convexity.

paragraphs: A graph model can struggle when the graph used for testing differs from the graph used for training. Differences can involve node features, labels, and the patterns of connections between nodes. Pair-Align addresses this graph domain adaptation problem by explicitly accounting for changes in structure and in the distribution of labels.

The method separates conditional structure shift from label shift. It handles the former by assigning edge weights that recalibrate how neighboring nodes influence one another. It handles the latter by weighting labels in the classification loss. These two adjustments connect the adaptation mechanism to different sources of mismatch, within an approach the authors describe as theoretically principled.

The paper reports superior performance for social-network node classification across regions and for pileup mitigation in particle-collision experiments, alongside strong synthetic and benchmark results. It also contributes a social-network dataset described as the largest for graph domain adaptation at the time of the study. The findings support adapting both neighborhood influence and label contributions when transferring models between graphs.
icml-2024-pairwise-alignment-improves-gr.tldr: Pair-Align improves graph transfer by reweighting edges for structural shifts and classification losses for label shifts.

paragraphs: Multi-view, multi-label learning combines several views of an example to predict multiple semantic tags. The challenge becomes harder when some views and labels are missing. This paper asks how to preserve useful agreement across views while ensuring that the shared representation remains relevant to the labels being predicted.

The method uses an information-bottleneck-based model to compress cross-view representations. It reduces information that is not shared across views while retaining valid features, aiming to increase the proportion of task-relevant information. It also represents multi-label prototype instances in latent space and learns label correlations from data, connecting the shared representation to relationships among the prediction targets.

The authors report better performance than existing state-of-the-art methods on multiple public datasets, with compatibility across both incomplete and complete data. Their experiments also emphasize that condensing shared information requires balancing what information is retained. The contribution therefore combines representation compression and prototype modeling, with evidence that concentrating shared information can improve classification when the process preserves useful predictive content.
icml-2024-partial-multi-view-multi-label.tldr: The method combines shared-information compression with latent prototypes to predict multiple labels despite missing views and labels.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that independent safety evaluation faces obstacles from the same company rules intended to prevent model misuse. Researchers may fear losing access or facing legal action for conducting good-faith investigations or publishing findings. The authors view those incentives as a barrier to identifying risks in generative AI systems.

They propose that major developers establish both legal and technical safe harbors for public-interest safety research. These commitments would remove threats of account suspension or legal reprisal for protected work. The paper also argues that company-run researcher access programs are inadequate substitutes because of limited community representation, insufficient funding, and dependence on corporate incentives.

The proposal draws on the authors’ collective experience studying safety, privacy, and trustworthiness. Their stated goal is to align research norms and incentives with public interests without worsening misuse. They present safe-harbor commitments as a necessary step toward broader, less obstructed community participation. The contribution is an institutional argument about enabling independent scrutiny, grounded in researchers’ experiences of existing access and enforcement practices.
icml-2024-position-a-safe-harbor-for-ai-.tldr: The authors call for legal and technical safe harbors that protect independent, good-faith AI safety research.

paragraphs: Foundation models depend heavily on large training collections assembled from many sources, often with poor documentation. This position paper connects those practices to difficulties verifying authenticity and consent, protecting privacy, understanding representation and bias, and respecting copyright. The authors treat training-data transparency as an important part of understanding model limitations and supporting trustworthy development.

The paper draws on a large-scale analysis of the training-data landscape and existing solutions. It examines weaknesses in common tools for recording authenticity, consent, and documentation, then identifies infrastructure that is missing from current practice. This frames the problem as one involving the systems used to track and describe data across its use in model development.

The authors advocate universal data-provenance standards and outline roles for policymakers, developers, and data creators in adopting them. Their contribution links a diagnosis of current documentation problems to a shared infrastructure proposal. The intended value is to make responsible development easier to support through consistent records of data origins and associated information, addressing transparency needs across the actors involved.
icml-2024-position-data-authenticity-con.tldr: The paper argues for universal data-provenance standards to address gaps in training-data authenticity, consent, and documentation.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that causal methods have considerable promise but face conflicting expectations that impede progress. One expectation is scientific perfectionism: using a causal model only when it can be regarded as correct. The authors contend that this stance slows the adoption of causal approaches in applications intended to generate knowledge.

A different pressure comes from computer science’s preference for algorithms requiring few assumptions, together with economic and business preferences for automation and scalability. The authors see these priorities as another obstacle to causal work. Their argument connects the difficulty of adoption to how different communities judge methods, rather than locating the issue solely in the methods themselves.

They propose a human-centered philosophy called scientific pragmatism to replace these system-centered biases. The call is for the machine learning community to find a balance that gives causal approaches room to contribute. As a position statement, the paper offers a framing for research priorities and adoption: progress depends partly on reconsidering the standards through which useful causal modeling is evaluated.
icml-2024-position-the-causal-revolution.tldr: The authors advocate human-centered scientific pragmatism to help causal methods advance amid conflicting expectations about correctness and automation.

paragraphs: Cross-domain recommendation uses information from different domains to address sparse data. Many approaches depend on shared users or items and access to their ratings or reviews across domains. This paper targets a more restrictive setting: improving recommendations in both source and target domains without overlapping users or items, while protecting data privacy.

The proposed RidCDR model uses a private, robust embedding-alignment module to share knowledge across domains. Alignment provides the mechanism for connecting their learned representations, while the robust design aims to avoid negative transfer, where shared information harms performance. Privacy protection and beneficial transfer are therefore treated together within the model’s cross-domain sharing component.

Experiments on Amazon and Douban datasets show RidCDR significantly outperforming state-of-the-art methods in the studied privacy-preserving setting without overlapping users or items. The stated findings support cross-domain learning under conditions that remove a common basis for matching domains. The contribution is especially relevant to the paper’s motivating problem: obtaining useful shared information when conventional access to common user–item records is unavailable.
icml-2024-reducing-item-discrepancy-via-.tldr: RidCDR aligns embeddings privately to improve cross-domain recommendations without requiring overlapping users or items.

paragraphs: Mean-field variational inference offers a relatively inexpensive way to approximate uncertainty over Bayesian neural-network weights. Its sampling process can nevertheless make training difficult: samples may poorly represent the most probable weights, and noisy gradient estimates can slow or disrupt optimization. This paper addresses those sampling difficulties through Reparameterized Importance Sampling, or RIS.

RIS estimates the first moment in neural networks while reducing variance during feed-forward propagation. The authors first analyze a generalized optimal proposal distribution and develop a computationally inexpensive approximation. They then express sampling from that proposal as a transformation combining external randomness with the variational parameters, making the sampling construction central to the learning method.

Experiments report better convergence, improved predictive performance, and successful uncertainty estimation for out-of-distribution data. These findings address both the optimization difficulties motivating the work and the quality of the resulting predictions and uncertainty estimates. The contribution is a targeted modification to sampling within variational Bayesian networks, supported by analysis of the proposal distribution and empirical evidence across those three outcomes.
icml-2024-reparameterized-importance-sam.tldr: RIS improves sampling in variational Bayesian neural networks, with reported gains in convergence, prediction, and out-of-distribution uncertainty estimation.

paragraphs: Class imbalance makes it difficult to generalize well on underrepresented examples. Removing examples from abundant classes or repeating scarce ones is common, but choosing between these strategies often relies on empirical testing. This paper develops a theoretical account of how sampling decisions should respond to the statistical properties of the data.

For linear support vector machines in a high-dimensional regime, the authors derive exact analytical expressions for generalization curves. They predict the effects of under- and oversampling using class imbalance, the data’s first and second moments, and the performance metric being considered. This makes the preferred sampling approach depend on more than the relative sizes of the classes.

The analysis shows that mixed strategies combining under- and oversampling can improve performance. Numerical experiments demonstrate the relevance of the theoretical predictions on real datasets, deeper architectures, and sampling approaches based on unsupervised probabilistic models. The exact theory applies to the stated linear-classifier setting, while the experiments provide evidence that its predictions can inform decisions in additional settings.
icml-2024-restoring-balance-principled-u.tldr: A high-dimensional theory of linear classifiers explains how data statistics and evaluation metrics should guide combined under- and oversampling.

paragraphs: SPHINX-X is a family of multimodal language models built by revising the SPHINX architecture and expanding its training data. The paper combines improvements to training efficiency with a study of models at different parameter scales. This creates a common framework for investigating how data and model size relate to multimodal performance.

The architecture removes redundant visual encoders, uses skip tokens for fully padded sub-images, and replaces multistage training with one combined stage. The authors assemble public language, vision, and vision-language resources, adding curated OCR-intensive and Set-of-Mark datasets. These changes address both the processing pipeline and the breadth of information available during training.

Training on TinyLlama-1.1B, InternLM2-7B, LLaMA2-13B, and Mixtral-8×7B produces models with different sizes and multilingual capabilities. Extensive benchmarking finds a strong correlation between multimodal performance and the scales of data and parameters. The finding describes an observed relationship across the evaluated family, while the broader contribution is a streamlined framework and expanded data collection for developing models across that range.
icml-2024-sphinx-x-scaling-data-and-para.tldr: SPHINX-X streamlines multimodal training and expands data, finding strong performance correlations with data and parameter scale.

paragraphs: Timer explores large pretrained models for time-series analysis, motivated by difficulties that smaller models encounter when task-specific data is scarce. The authors argue that saturated benchmarks can hide these difficulties. Their aim is to move beyond training a separate small model from scratch for each scenario toward a model that can be adapted across tasks.

The study curates pretraining datasets containing up to one billion time points and converts heterogeneous series into a common single-series sequence format. It then develops a GPT-style transformer trained through next-token prediction. Forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection are reformulated as generative tasks so that the same modeling approach can address these different application needs.

The resulting Time Series Transformer, Timer, is adapted to downstream tasks and shows promising capabilities as a large time-series model. The contribution is presented as an early development of this direction. It brings together data preparation, a shared sequence format, generative pretraining, and task reformulation to explore how one pretrained architecture can support several kinds of time-series analysis.
icml-2024-timer-generative-pre-trained-t.tldr: Timer uses large-scale generative pretraining and a unified sequence format to support forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection.
